content: The development of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) is likely influenced by multiple factors, and its exact mechanisms are not fully understood. In individuals with asthma, inflammation plays a significant role in the pathogenesis of EIB. However, the role of inflammation appears to be less pronounced in individuals without asthma. The management of EIB primarily focuses on prevention, which can involve both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic strategies. This review aimed to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in treating EIB. Specifically, it sought to determine whether ICS, when compared to placebo, could reduce the severity of EIB in both adult and pediatric patients with asthma. Additionally, the review aimed to quantify the extent of this effect. To gather relevant data, the researchers searched multiple sources, including the Cochrane Airways Review Group Specialised Register of trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, review articles, textbooks, and reference lists of related studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized trials involving adults or children that compared ICS with placebo for the prevention of EIB. The quality of the trials and the extraction of data were independently assessed by two reviewers. The analysis included data from eight randomized controlled trials, which involved a total of 162 participants. Of these, two trials focused on adults, while six involved children. When the results of three parallel studies with a minimum ICS treatment duration of four weeks were combined, the use of ICS was found to significantly reduce the percentage decline in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) following exercise. The weighted mean difference (WMD) for this reduction was 11.74% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.06% to 13.42%). In one crossover study, which also involved a four-week duration of ICS treatment, significant reductions were observed in both the percentage decline in FEV1 (WMD: 11.70%; 95% CI: 7.51% to 15.90%) and the percentage decline in peak expiratory flow (PEF) (WMD: 11.50%; 95% CI: 6.31% to 16.69%). However, the limited data from placebo-controlled trials that used a single treatment session did not provide sufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions. The authors concluded that the use of ICS for at least four weeks prior to exercise testing significantly reduced the severity of EIB. However, the relative efficacy of ICS compared to other treatments for EIB, such as sodium cromoglycate, nedocromil sodium, salbutamol, or other anti-inflammatory agents, remains uncertain.
